# Assembled standards

**These are the documents to read.** Everything here is generated by
`tools/build-standard.js` from the individual part files one directory up, and
every one of them is whole and self-contained — start at the top and read
down.

| Document | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| [`FRONTEND-ARCHITECTURE-STANDARD.md`](./FRONTEND-ARCHITECTURE-STANDARD.md) | The frontend rulebook, end to end: principles, folder shape, layer boundaries, naming, size, state, types, the API layer, documentation, testing, git flow and the migration approach. |
| [`CODE-DOCUMENTATION-STANDARD.md`](./CODE-DOCUMENTATION-STANDARD.md) | How code documents itself, on its own, for a reader who is not reading the frontend standard. |

## Do not edit anything in this folder

A file here is an output. Editing one changes nothing anybody else reads and
is overwritten the next time the script runs — the `no-edit-generated-docs`
rule asks before letting a write land on one, for exactly that reason.

Edit the part one directory up instead, then regenerate:

```
node tools/build-standard.js
```

`npm run build:check` verifies that what is committed here still matches what
the parts produce, and the test suite fails if it has drifted.

## Why the split exists at all

A part is small enough to argue about, review, and own on its own; a whole
document is what someone actually reads when they want to understand the
standard rather than look one rule up. Keeping the two in separate folders
means the difference is visible from the path, rather than from noticing
which filenames happen to be upper-case.

One part can feed more than one document. `code-documentation.md` is a
section of the frontend standard *and* the whole of the documentation
standard; editing it once updates both, and neither ever holds a
hand-maintained copy of the other.
